title: Favorite trombone players and other musicians
summary: Asked for favorites, he names J.J. Johnson and Kai Winding for bebop and Roy Palmer for old New Orleans, with Dickie Wells and others, plus brief talk of Oliver's eye.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: I was going to ask you, I don't want to put you on the spot, but I mean if you don't mind saying who would be your favorite trombone player. There's nothing wrong with having a favorite, I mean that's not insulting the other people, because I know you like a lot of them, you told me you liked a whole bunch of them. Well if you had to pick one or two.

Well if I had to pick a trombone player, these modern day trombone players, I'd have to pick them from the style. Now for that bebop, I like some of it, some of it I don't. But for the bebop, there's K. Wenge and there's J.J. Johnson, there's two best. I mean of the old times, your whole life, it's the best you ever heard.

Oh you're just talking about the old music, or the old music, or just everybody. Just everybody in the world. Well that's kind of hard because we had a boy that called Big Green. And for playing blues, according to what kind of music played, for playing blues, Big Green, and I love Vic, and it's just, it's kind of hard. The old time. And that was Roy, I'd put Roy against any of them. And that was Jimmy Harrison, I heard him but I never saw him. I didn't hear much of him though. But going from what Lou and them boys say, and the look that I heard of him, it's kind of hard. And there's T. Gordon, he plays so much trombone player, so much trombone, a wonderful trombone player, I'd be afraid to say I was too good. I don't know, I was, just like I said, this boy for execution, this bebop, this J.J. and this K. Windy, for that style, it was the best I ever heard. I never heard fellas get off. I think they're playing valves though. Must be. Yeah, they must be, for that execution. See I never saw them just in person playing. So I don't know whether they're playing valves or the slide. So but I'd pick, for the old musician, the old New Orleans musician, I'd pick Roy Palmer. I'd take Roy Palmer. Maybe I'm a bit prejudiced. I'd pick him over Detroit. Dutrae taught me too. But Dutrae didn't play as much as he did. Now O'Reay played a whole lot too, but not as much as Roy Palmer. He didn't seem to care much about Roy Palmer.
I wonder why. Well he never made a lot of records.
No, he didn't seem to care much about that.
Maybe it was the way Roy Carriott still. I just had to be a football player. Maybe he had the reputation of going to sleep on a job or something, you know?
Yeah, and I just felt like Dickie Wells, he was a wonderful trombone player. He still plays.

I was going to ask again, before I forget it, about Joe Oliver again. Was he really a good pool player? Did he play all the time? Who was that? Joe Oliver. Oh yeah, he was good. You know he had one bad eye.

And he's good, a good pool player. Yeah. He had one bad idea. Now you take Armani for the type of music that he played, he was all right. But I wouldn't put him in the same category as Earl Hines. And there's Teddy Wilson. Now there's Kate Johnson, another trombone player where he's playing, Bud Johnson's brother. He was wonderful I think too. After immediately he was Armstrong, he joined Armstrong. And he played some wonderful solos, breaks and things. So I mean there's so many. And there's Vic. Vic got a style all his own. That's Lawrence Brown. I mean there's so many. And nowadays they're jumping up. These youngsters are playing, they seem to have so much more execution.
